newsitem.title: INDIA: India suggests China model for Pakistan talks.
newsitem.headline: India suggests China model for Pakistan talks.

text.p: Indian Foreign Minister Inder Gujral said on Thursday that forthcoming peace talks with Pakistan could benefit from the example set by New Delhi's border negotiations with China.
"No two sovereign nations can agree 100 percent to the other person's point of view," Gujral told India's Asian News International news agency.

"We have made progress in the India-China relationship which was far more involved and far more difficult," he said, referring to issues to be discussed with Pakistan in bilateral talks between foreign secretaries starting on March 28.
India and China fought a brief border war over their Himalayan frontier in 1962, freezing relations between the Asian giants for more than 25 years.
Ties improved in 1988 when then-Indian prime minister Rajiv Gandhi visited Beijing to begin a lengthy process of negotiations over the vast border.
They signed a treaty along the poorly demarcated boundary in 1993, while senior defence and foreign ministry officials were asked to continue to work on potentially difficult solutions.

"On the most contentious issue like the borders, both countries have been working for more than 10 years, and we are inching towards a settlement. That is what is indicated in the confidence-building measures," Gujral said.
Gujral said India and China had succeeded with their talks in creating an atmosphere of trust and confidence.
"It is that atmosphere which helps in sorting things out," he said. "I do not expect miracles, but I do hope that we will see sense, both of us."
The foreign secretaries' meeting from March 28 to 31 would mark the resumption of Indo-Pakistani peace talks which broke off in January 1994.

Gujral said on Wednesday that the talks would be followed by meetings between the foreign ministers in early April, and the prime ministers of the two countries will meet on the margins of a regional summit in May.
He said Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda will meet his Pakistani counterpart, Nawaz Sharif, during a summit in May of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC).

A Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesman said it was premature to say whether the two prime ministers would have bilateral talks. He said Pakistan had not yet received a formal invitation from the Maldives to attend the South Asian summit.
Despite the breakdown in the official talks in 1994, Indian and Pakistani leaders have occasionally met on the sidelines of international conferences.

Pakistani President Farooq Khan Leghari met then-prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao during the SAARC summit in New Delhi in May 1995 when they discussed but failed to make any headway on a dispute over Kashmir.

Two thirds of Kashmir is ruled by India and the rest by Pakistan. More than 20,000 people have died in Jammu and Kashmir since 1990 when simmering discontent against New Delhi's rule there turned into an armed insurrection.
